opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. The uses that have stuck with me most are the ones where people stop treating the model as a black box they poke from the outside and start looking at what's going on inside it.

The first is debugging behavior. Someone has a model doing something weird: it's sycophantic in a particular context, or it refuses things it shouldn't, or it quietly picks up a bias from the training data. Normally you'd tweak the prompt, add more fine-tuning data, and hope. With Silico you can find the internal features that light up when the behavior happens and ask, "What concept is the model actually using here?" Sometimes the answer surprises you. The model is keying off something you never would have guessed from the outputs alone. That changes how you fix it, because you're fixing the cause instead of patching symptoms.

The second is steering. Once you've found a feature that corresponds to something meaningful, like a tone, a topic, or a style of reasoning, you can turn it up or down directly. That's a much more precise lever than prompting. It's also a great way to check your understanding: if you think a feature means X, intervene on it and see whether the behavior changes the way you'd predict. If it doesn't, you've learned you were wrong, which is just as valuable.

The third, and honestly the one I find most exciting, is scientific discovery. People are training models on biological or other scientific data, and those models get very good at prediction while nobody knows what they've learned. Being able to open them up and pull out the concepts they've formed means the model isn't just a prediction engine but a source of new hypotheses. You're learning something about the world from what the model figured out.

What ties these together is a shift in the relationship between people and the models. Instead of "we trained it and it works, mostly, and we don't really know why," it becomes something you can inspect, reason about, and edit deliberately. That's the direction I think the whole field needs to go, and it's been really fun to watch people find uses we didn't anticipate when we built it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the ones that have surprised me most are the cases where people use Silico less as a replacement for a real study and more as a way to think before they run one. A product team will come in with a survey they've already drafted, and instead of fielding it to two thousand people, they run it against a simulated population first. Nine times out of ten they discover the question is confusing, or the answer options don't cover the thing people actually care about, or there's a whole segment reacting in a way nobody anticipated. That's cheap to find out in silico and expensive to find out after you've spent six weeks and a lot of money.

The second category I find compelling is exploring the space of possibilities that you'd never get budget to test. Say you have a pricing change and you want to know how it lands with fifteen different customer profiles across a dozen message framings. No one is going to run a hundred and eighty-cell study. But you can simulate it, look at where the signal is strong, and then spend your real research dollars on the two or three cells that actually matter. It's a filter, not a verdict.

And then there's the stuff that's harder to describe, which is using it as a kind of intuition pump. Founders especially will sit with it and interrogate a simulated customer the way they'd never be able to with a real one, because a real one gets tired, or polite, or wants to leave. You can ask the same thing ten different ways and watch where the answer changes. I'm careful about this one, because it's easy to mistake a plausible-sounding answer for a true one. But as a way of generating hypotheses you then go verify with real humans, I think it's genuinely useful, and it's the use I'd point to if someone asked me what the tool is actually for.

astra-6.text:
The uses I find most compelling are the ones where someone wants to understand how different people might respond to an idea before they commit to it. That could be a product decision or how you communicate something. You have an intuition, but you want to explore where that intuition might break down.

What’s interesting is being able to ask, “Who might see this differently, and why?” That can surface a concern or a perspective you hadn’t considered. I think that’s a useful way to approach it: as a way to generate hypotheses and make the questions you eventually ask real people much better.
